title: Healthy leaf
what_it_means: No disease was found on this leaf.
what_to_do: Keep checking the crop once a week. Keep the field clean, remove weeds and fallen leaves, and water at the base of the plant.
source: General crop-hygiene guidance - TO CITE (ICAR / TNAU package of practices)

title: Fungal disease
what_it_means: A fungus is attacking the leaf. Fungi spread through spores in wind and water splashes, mostly in humid weather.
what_to_do: Remove and destroy badly infected leaves (do not compost them). Avoid wetting the leaves when watering and give plants space for air flow. If it keeps spreading, use a fungicide that is registered (CIB&RC) for this crop and this disease, at the dose and waiting period written on the label. Ask your KVK which product to use.
source: TO CITE (ICAR / TNAU package of practices)

title: Late blight (oomycete)
what_it_means: A water-mould (Phytophthora) is attacking the plant. It can destroy a whole field in a few days in cool, wet weather.
what_to_do: Act today. Remove infected plants and leaves and keep them out of the field. Ordinary fungicides may not work: use a product registered (CIB&RC) for late blight on this crop, exactly as the label says. Contact your KVK or agriculture officer quickly.
source: TO CITE (ICAR / TNAU package of practices)

title: Bacterial disease
what_it_means: Bacteria are attacking the leaf. They spread with water, hands and tools. Fungicides alone do not stop bacteria.
what_to_do: Remove infected leaves. Do not work among plants while they are wet and clean your tools. Use disease-free seed or seedlings next season. A copper-based product registered (CIB&RC) for this crop can slow it down - follow the label. Ask your KVK.
source: TO CITE (ICAR / TNAU package of practices)

title: Viral / systemic disease
what_it_means: A virus (or, for citrus greening, a bacterium inside the plant) is in the whole plant. No spray can cure an infected plant.
what_to_do: Pull out and destroy infected plants so they do not infect others. Control the insects that spread it (whiteflies, aphids, psyllids) - ask your KVK for a registered method. Next season use resistant varieties and healthy seedlings.
source: TO CITE (ICAR / TNAU package of practices)

title: Mite attack
what_it_means: Tiny spider mites are feeding on the leaf, usually on its underside. They grow fast in hot, dry weather.
what_to_do: Look under the leaves for mites and fine webs. Spraying water under the leaves can knock them off. If many plants are attacked, use an acaricide registered (CIB&RC) for this crop, as the label says. Avoid strong insecticides that also kill the insects that eat mites.
source: TO CITE (ICAR / TNAU package of practices)

title: Please ask an expert
what_it_means: The model could not narrow the problem down to one kind of treatment. Giving advice now could mean using the wrong treatment.
what_to_do: Take the leaf (or clear photos of it) to your nearest Krishi Vigyan Kendra (KVK) or agriculture officer. Do not spray anything until the cause is known.

title: Photo not recognised
what_it_means: This photo does not look like the leaves the model was trained on. It may be another crop, not a leaf, or a very unclear photo.
what_to_do: Take a new, sharp photo of ONE leaf in daylight, filling most of the picture. Supported crops: apple, blueberry, cherry, corn, grape, orange, peach, bell pepper, potato, raspberry, soybean, squash, strawberry, tomato.
